messages.content: my grandmother taught me a song when i was little. now i want to teach it to my daughter, but i only remember part of it.
you can begin with the part you remember and tell your daughter where you learned it. you do not have to say you know the whole song.
i want a short way to say that before we sing.
my grandmother taught me this song when i was little. i only remember part of it, but i would like to share that part with you.
can we make up the part i forgot together?
yes. you can make up a new part together while keeping it clear that those words are yours. the new part can become something you and your daughter share.
write a short conversation where she asks about that.
did your grandmother sing these words? she taught me the first part. we made up the last part together. then it is our song too? yes, we kept something old and added something new.
what did grandmother teach me, and what did i add?
she taught you the old song. you and your daughter added a new part because you did not remember all of the old one.
use drinking and studying in a short story about my brother. it can be made up.

my brother is studying at the kitchen table. he has a book, a page for writing, and a glass of water. while he is drinking, he looks at a question in the book. he puts the glass down before writing his answer. when he finishes that part, he stands up and takes a short break.
what was he drinking?
he was drinking water.
can you write the story about yesterday instead?

yesterday, my brother was studying at the kitchen table. he had a book, a page for writing, and a glass of water. while he was drinking, he looked at a question in the book. he put the glass down before writing his answer. when he finished that part, he stood up and took a short break.
did he finish the whole book?
the story only says that he finished one part. it does not say that he finished the whole book.
make the last part say that he went back to study after the break.
after the break, he returned to the table, opened the book again, and began the next part.
a doctor came to our house for dinner because she is a friend of my mother. does that mean the visit was about health?
no. you said she came for dinner as a friend. a person who works as a doctor can visit friends without doing work at that visit.
can you ask my question in fewer words?
was the visit for dinner or about health?
write a short story with the doctor talking about books at dinner.

a doctor visits a friend for dinner. they sit at the kitchen table with the family and talk about books. the child asks which story she likes best. she says that she enjoys stories about a long journey. after dinner, the child brings a book from another room and asks if she has read it.
did she answer the question about the book?
not yet. the story stops after the child asks it. we do not know whether she has read that book.
finish with her saying she has not read it and asking what it is about.
she says: i have not read that one. what is it about? the child sits near her and starts to tell the story.
my uncle works at a bank. if i meet him outside the bank after work, am i working there too?
no. meeting someone outside a place does not mean you work there. you could be there just to meet your uncle.
write a small story where we walk home together after that meeting.

i wait outside the bank until my uncle finishes work. he comes through the door and sees me near a tree. we walk home together and talk about our day. when we reach the house, he puts his things by the door, and i go to the kitchen for water.
who works at the bank in that story?
your uncle works there. the story only says that you wait outside for him.
if i say we left the bank together, does that mean we both worked there?
no. leaving together only says that you went away from that place together. it does not give the reason each person was there.
can you keep the meeting story but write it using she for me?
she waits outside the bank until her uncle finishes work. he sees her near a tree, and they walk home together. they talk about their day along the way.
i see ice and cream in ice cream. is that always a list of two different things?
no. ice cream is used as a name for one kind of food. putting words together can give a meaning that is different from reading each word alone.
give me a short conversation about choosing it after lunch.
would you like something after lunch? yes, i would like ice cream. do you want it now? no, i am still full. could i have it later? yes, we can keep it for later.
who is full?
the person asking for ice cream is full. they want it, but they do not want it right after lunch.
if i just say cream, do i always mean ice cream?
no. cream can be used by itself for something different. the word ice is part of the name ice cream, so leaving it out can change what you are asking for.
write a clear request for the whole food name.
could i have some ice cream later, please?
can i answer that with just yes in a simple conversation?
yes. if the request is clear and you are saying they can have it, yes can be enough.
write a story with arm and hand. a person is carrying books and needs help with a door.

a woman holds three books with one arm. her other hand is holding a small container. she comes to a closed door and needs help opening it. a man near the door asks whether she wants help. she says yes and asks him to open the door. he holds it while she walks through. she thanks him and puts the books on a desk inside.
make the story a little shorter.

a woman holds three books with one arm and a container in her other hand. she comes to a closed door. a man near the door asks whether she wants help. she asks him to open it. he holds the door while she carries her things inside.
did he carry the books for her?
no. she carried the books through the door herself. he helped by opening and holding the door.
change it so he asks before taking anything from her.
he asks: would you like me to open the door or carry something? she says: please open the door. i can carry these things myself.
why is that question useful?
it helps her say which help she wants, rather than having him choose for her.
help me use eye and ear in a simple story without making it about health.

a child draws a face on a page. she draws one eye and one ear. her brother asks why there is only one of each. she says that we see the face from one side in the picture. he looks at the side of his own head in a mirror.
can you tell it in fewer words?
a child draws one side of a face, with one eye and one ear. her brother asks why there is only one of each. she says that we see just one side in the picture.
does having one eye in the picture mean the person only has one eye?
no. a picture can show only one side of a person. a part that is not in the picture is not always a part that is gone.
write a question the brother could ask instead of saying the drawing is wrong.
are we looking at the face from the side?
what does that question check?
it asks which part of the face we see in the drawing.
tell me the difference between he rides the train and he rode the train.
he rides the train can be about something he does now or often. he rode the train is about a time in the past.
use yesterday and every week to make the difference clear.
he rides the train every week. he rode the train yesterday.
can both sentences be about the same person?
yes. he can take the train every week and have taken it yesterday too. one sentence is general, and the other is about yesterday.
explain the difference in fewer words.
every week is general. yesterday is one specific day in the past. both can be true about the same person.
write a short story using rode, ran, and waited.
yesterday, he rode the train to town. after leaving the station, he ran to the library because he wanted to meet his sister. she had not come yet, so he waited near the door.
does running tell us whether he was late?
no. he could run for more than one reason. the story says that he wanted to meet his sister, but it does not say that he was late.
write a short story with watches and builds. let a child make something while a parent watches.

a child builds a small house with pieces from a toy. his mother watches from the table while drinking tea. he makes a door and a roof, then asks whether she likes it. she says that she likes the way he made space for a window. he puts the house near her cup so she can see inside it.
what does the child build?
he builds a small toy house.
does watches mean she does the building for him?
no. watches says that she looks at what he is doing. the story says that the child builds the house himself.
change the story so she helps only after he asks.

a child builds a small house with pieces from a toy. his mother watches while drinking tea. when he cannot make the roof stay in place, he asks for help. she holds one side while he puts another piece in place. then he takes his hand away, and the roof is still there.
make the last part simple.
she holds one side while he puts another piece in place. then he takes his hand away, and the roof is still there.
my aunt said she will visit next month. can i tell my brother that she is coming tomorrow?
not from that information alone. next month does not give a specific day. tomorrow could be part of next month at the end of a month, but you still need to know when she plans to come.
i want a short message that keeps the time general.
our aunt plans to visit next month. we do not know the day yet.
she also said she will bring a book for us. add that.
our aunt plans to visit next month and bring a book for us. we do not know the day yet.
does that mean a book for each of us?
not always. a book for us could mean one book to share. ask her if you need to know how many.
answer in fewer words.
no. it could be one book to share.
write a question asking both the day and the number of books.
what day do you plan to come, and are you bringing one book for us to share?
my friend began to cry while we were reading. i do not know why. help me ask a kind question.
you could say: would you like to tell me what you are feeling, or would you rather have a quiet moment?
should i say that the story made them sad?
not if you do not know. the story might be part of the reason, but something else could be on their mind. asking leaves room for them to tell you.
they say they remembered their grandmother reading the same book.
then they have told you about a memory the book brought back. you could reply: thank you for telling me. would you like to talk about her?
i want to keep reading with them if they want to. add that choice.
thank you for telling me. we can talk about her, keep reading, or sit quietly for a while. what would you like?
what if they do not want to choose right away?
you can give them time: that is okay. we do not have to choose now.
does that tell us whether the memory is happy or sad?
no. a person can cry with different feelings. your friend has not said which feeling they have.
i like bread with butter, but today i wanted it without butter. is that a change in what i like?
not always. you can like bread with butter and still choose bread without it today.
say that in fewer words.
you can like butter and choose not to have it at one meal.
write a small conversation at breakfast.
would you like butter on your bread? not today, thank you. i thought you liked it. i do. i just want bread without butter this morning.
keep only the last reply.
i do. i just want bread without butter this morning.
can i say the person does not like butter?
no. the person says they like it. choosing not to have it this morning does not mean they hate it.
write it in one sentence.
the person likes butter but wants bread without it this morning.
a picture has three vehicles. one is red and two are blue. does the picture tell me that all three are the same kind?
not from those details. vehicle is a general word. knowing the number and color does not tell you whether they are all the same kind of vehicle.
if two look the same, does that make the red one different?
no. the red vehicle could have the same shape as the two blue vehicles. a different color alone does not tell us that it is a different kind.
say that in fewer words.
no. color alone does not tell us whether it is a different kind of vehicle.
write two sentences using only the facts i first gave.
there are three vehicles in the picture. one is red, and two are blue.
now make a story where a child draws them.
a child draws three vehicles on a page. she makes one red and two blue. her father asks where they are going. she says they are all going to the same town, but the road is not on the page yet.
did the first two sentences say anything about a town?
no. the town was added for the made up story.
use level in a simple sentence about a game.
she has finished the first level of the game and is ready for the next one.
did she finish the whole game?
not from that sentence alone. she finished the first level, and there is another part for her to try.
write a short story where she learns something in that first level.
a girl starts a new game. the first level is easy and helps her learn how to move the objects. she tries a few choices and sees what happens. in the next level, she can use what she learned before.
can she still need help in the next level?
yes. learning one part does not mean she already knows everything about the game. the next part may give her something new to learn.
let her ask her brother for help without asking him to play for her.
can you explain this rule to me? i want to do the next part myself, but i do not understand what i should do first.
write his reply if he wants her to show what she has tried.
show me what you have tried so far. then we can look at the rule together.
hey, can you help me write a short message to my cousin?
hey. what do you want the message to say?
i left a book at their house and want to know if they can find it. it might be under the table.
you could write: hey, did i leave my book at your house? it might be under the table. could you look when you have time?
i know i left it there. do not ask if i did.
hey, i left my book at your house. it might be under the table. could you look when you have time?
can i use hey when writing to a teacher?
if you are not sure how to start, hello is a simple choice for your teacher.
give me just that first word.
hello.
now write the cousin message without hey or hello.
i left my book at your house. it might be under the table. could you look when you have time?
if we say we made it ourselves, does that mean each person worked alone?
no. ourselves can be about a group doing something together. we made it ourselves can mean that the people in the group did the work without having someone else make it for them.
write a story about two friends making a card themselves.

two friends want to make a card for their teacher. one draws a picture while the other writes a message. they choose the color together and put both parts on the same page. when the teacher asks where the card came from, they say they made it themselves.
did both people write the message?
the story says that one wrote the message and the other drew the picture. they both helped with the card, but they did not do the same task.
can they both say i helped make it?
yes. each did part of the work, so each can say that they helped make the card.
change it so they ask a parent to write the message, but still draw the picture themselves.
the two friends draw a picture together and ask a parent to write the message. they make the card with help, rather than doing every part themselves.
